Indexed Performance

Indexed Vol Normalized Performance

The same funds, each rescaled to 10% annualized volatility. Raw performance mixes skill with risk taken — a fund running twice the volatility should earn twice the return for that alone. Here every line carries the same risk, so the ending value is the risk-adjusted ranking. Scaling is recomputed per timeframe; hover shows each fund's realized vol, applied factor and funding cost.

Funding costs are included: scaling the excess return is the same as holding the fund at k times its size and financing the extra (k−1) at the 2.0% risk-free rate. Over the full window this ranges from +1.32%/yr for Global Agg Bond USD-H (k = 1.66×, the most levered) down to -1.28%/yr for Gold (k = 0.36× — de-levered funds hold the unused cash and earn the rate instead of paying it). Real financing is dearer than the risk-free rate, so this is a floor.

Maximum Diversification — 5 assets

Holding no more than 5 funds, which ones combine into the least concentrated book? Two measures are reported side by side because they answer different questions:

DR (diversification ratio) = weighted-average vol / portfolio vol. Maximising it is mathematically the same as a minimum-variance problem in correlation space, so it spreads risk rather than capital — and it will happily pile into the lowest-vol asset, which is why the unconstrained optimum tends to be bond-heavy.
ENB (effective number of bets) = entropy of risk across the uncorrelated principal components. This is the one that takes “as orthogonal as possible” literally: ENB = 1 means all risk rides on a single factor, ENB = 5 means it is spread evenly over 5 independent sources. A high DR with a low ENB is low volatility concentrated in one risk source — not what you want.

Weight floors matter: without one, a “5-asset” optimum can put 2% in a holding and really be a 3-asset portfolio. The min 10% row shows what insisting on a genuine 5-asset book costs in DR and buys in return.
